title: お〜する・ご〜する (humble)
meaning: Makes your own action sound humble in order to show respect to the other person. Typically used when you do something for them.
connection: お + verb masu-stem + する／ご + Sino-Japanese action noun + する

senses.label: お + native Japanese verb
senses.meaning: Lowers your own action to show respect. Roughly “Let me … for you.” The action usually involves the other person (done for them or toward them).
senses.connection: お + verb masu-stem + する／します (お持ちする, お待ちする, お送りする, お知らせする)
examples: Let me carry your bags.
Shall I take you to the station?
We will let you know the results by email at a later date.

senses.label: ご + Sino-Japanese noun
senses.meaning: Sino-Japanese words (on-reading words, kango) usually take 「ご」. The meaning is the same. Common in business: guiding, explaining, contacting.
senses.connection: ご + Sino-Japanese action noun + する (ご案内する, ご説明する, ご連絡する, ご紹介する)
examples: I'll show you to the meeting room.
Let me explain our new service.
I'll contact you again tomorrow.

senses.label: More formal forms
senses.meaning: Replace 「する」 with 「いたす」 for an even humbler tone. This is the most common choice with clients and in formal settings. 「お〜申し上げる」 is more formal still, mostly in letters and speeches.
senses.connection: お／ご〜いたします; お／ご〜申し上げます (お待ちしております, お願い申し上げます)
examples: We sincerely look forward to your visit.
Thank you very much for your kind cooperation.

notes: Use it only for actions by you or your side. Using it for the other person's action lowers them and is very rude: ✕「お客様がお待ちしています」→ ○「お客様がお待ちになっています」.

When telling a customer something "can be used", ✕「このカードはご利用できます」 is the potential form of the humble pattern, so it literally says the customer will "humbly use" it. This is the most common honorific mistake in business → ○「ご利用になれます」「ご利用いただけます」.
Verbs with special humble forms don't follow the formula: ✕「お見しする」「お言いする」「お行きする」→ ○「拝見する」「申し上げる」「伺う」.
The action must involve the other person (done for them or toward them). Purely personal actions can't take it: ✕「私は毎朝お走りします」→ ○「私は毎朝走っています」.

etymology: The prefixes 「お」 and 「ご」 come from 「御」, which originally showed respect for things belonging to the other person. Put on an action and followed by 「する」, they became a humble expression: “(I) do something for you.” 「お」 tends to go with native words and 「ご」 with Sino-Japanese words, the same split as in polite nouns.
formation: 「お／ご」 was originally the honorific prefix 「御」, attached to things belonging to the other person to show respect. The verb's masu-stem works as a noun for the action (「待ち」 and 「持ち」 can be used as nouns on their own), and 「する」 means "to do". Put together, it literally says "I do a (you-related) thing": your own action is turned into a noun, packaged as "something done for you", and then you "do" it. This creates a humble stance centered on the other person, with yourself placed lower. Because 「お」 points to the other person, the pattern naturally requires the action to involve them; purely personal actions don't fit. Replacing 「する」 with the humbler 「いたす」 or 「申し上げる」 raises the level of humility accordingly.

similar.title: 参る・申す・いたす (special humble verbs)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both are humble language. 「参る」, 「申す」, 「拝見する」 and the like are fixed special forms of certain verbs; when a special form exists, use it first. 「お〜する」 is the general formula for all other verbs. For 「見る」 say 「拝見する」, not 「お見しする」.

similar.title: 〜お〜申し上げる・ご〜申し上げる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: same structure, but replacing 「する」 with 「申し上げる」 makes it humbler and more formal. It is mostly used in letters, speeches and formal thanks or apologies, e.g. 「お祝い申し上げます」. In everyday spoken business Japanese, 「お〜します／いたします」 is enough.

similar.title: 〜お〜いただく・ご〜いただく
similar.explanation: Same origin: also a humble expression built from 「お／ご」 + verb, but the doer is different. 「お〜する」 is "I do it for you"; 「お〜いただく」 is "I humbly receive your doing it for me". 「ご説明します」 (I'll explain)／「ご説明いただきました」 (you kindly explained).

similar.title: お〜になる
similar.explanation: Same origin: also built from 「お」 + masu-stem, but 「お〜になる」 is respectful and used for the other person's actions. 「お持ちします」 (I'll carry it for you)／「お持ちになりますか」 (will you take it with you?). Mixing the two up is the quickest way to be rude.

title: いらっしゃる・おっしゃる (special respectful verbs)
meaning: Some common verbs have their own respectful forms. They raise the actions of the listener or the person being talked about.
connection: Replace the original verb (行く・来る・いる→いらっしゃる, 言う→おっしゃる, etc.)

senses.label: いらっしゃる
senses.meaning: Respectful form of 「行く」, 「来る」, and 「いる」. Context tells you which. The masu-form is 「いらっしゃいます」 (not 「いらっしゃります」).
senses.connection: いらっしゃる／いらっしゃいます／いらっしゃった; 〜ていらっしゃる (respectful 〜ている)
examples: The president is in the meeting room now.
I hear the teacher is going to Kyoto tomorrow.
Welcome! (Thank you for coming.)

senses.label: おっしゃる
senses.meaning: Respectful form of 「言う」. Used for what the listener or a superior says. The masu-form is 「おっしゃいます」.
senses.connection: おっしゃる／おっしゃいます／おっしゃった; 〜とおっしゃる
examples: It's exactly as you said, sir.
May I ask your name?

senses.label: 召し上がる・ご覧になる
senses.meaning: 「召し上がる」 is the respectful form of 「食べる」 and 「飲む」; 「ご覧になる」 is the respectful form of 「見る」. Often used to invite someone to eat, drink, or look.
senses.connection: 召し上がる／召し上がってください; ご覧になる／ご覧ください
examples: Please eat it while it's warm.
Please take a look at these materials.
Have you seen this movie yet?

senses.label: なさる・ご存じ
senses.meaning: 「なさる」 is the respectful form of 「する」; its masu-form is 「なさいます」. 「ご存じだ」 is the respectful form of 「知っている」; the negative is 「ご存じない」.
senses.connection: なさる／なさいます／なさった; ご存じです／ご存じですか
examples: What are you doing this weekend?
Do you know about this matter?

notes: Use them only for the listener or a third person. Using them for yourself means raising yourself up, which is very rude: ✕「私が先ほどおっしゃったとおり」→ ○「私が先ほど申し上げたとおり」; ✕「明日私がいらっしゃいます」→ ○「明日私が参ります」.
In the masu-form, 「る」 becomes 「い」: ○「いらっしゃいます」「おっしゃいます」「なさいます」, ✕「いらっしゃります」「おっしゃります」.
Don't stack 「れる・られる」 on top; that creates a double honorific: ✕「おっしゃられる」「召し上がられる」「ご覧になられる」→ ○「おっしゃる」「召し上がる」「ご覧になる」.
When talking to people outside your company about your own boss, don't use respectful language: ✕ (to a client)「部長は今、外出していらっしゃいます」→ ○「部長の田中はただいま外出しております」.

etymology: Most of these are old honorific verbs still in use. 「おっしゃる」 comes from a sound change of 「仰せある」. 「いらっしゃる」 comes from 「入らせらる」 (one theory). 「召し上がる」 combines 「召す」 (to summon; to partake) with 「上がる」. 「なさる」 comes from an honorific form of 「為す」.
formation: These verbs aren't assembled by a grammar formula. Instead, the original verb is replaced entirely by a different word that already means "an action of a superior". 「おっしゃる」 comes from 「仰せある」, where 「仰せ」 means "(a superior's) command or words"; 「召し上がる」 is 「召す」 (a noble person takes or uses) + 「上がる」; 「なさる」 is the honorific form of 「為す」; and 「いらっしゃる」 is said to come from 「入らせらる」. Because "the other person is of high rank" is built into their meaning, they can only be used for others; using them for yourself means raising yourself. Their masu-forms end in 「〜います」, generally explained as a sound change of the 「り」 in 「〜ります」, so they need to be memorized.

similar.title: 参る・申す・いたす (special humble verbs)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: they also replace verbs like 「行く」, 「言う」 and 「する」 with special verbs, but in the opposite direction: respectful verbs raise the other person's actions, humble verbs lower your own. 「先生がおっしゃる」／「私が申す」. Mixing them up is very rude.

similar.title: お〜になる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both are respectful language. Use the formula 「お〜になる」 only for verbs without a special form, e.g. 「お帰りになる」; when a special form exists, use it: ✕「お言いになる」→ ○「おっしゃる」.

similar.title: 〜れる・〜られる (respectful)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「言われる」 and 「来られる」 are also respectful, but the respect is lighter and they are easily confused with the passive. With superiors and clients, 「おっしゃる」 and 「いらっしゃる」 are more appropriate.

similar.title: 〜さしあげる・いただく・くださる (honorific giving and receiving)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「くださる」 (respectful form of 「くれる」) also belongs to this group of special respectful verbs, and its masu-form is likewise 「くださいます」. Honorific giving and receiving also includes humble verbs like 「さしあげる」 and 「いただく」; choose according to the direction of giving.

title: 参る・申す・いたす (special humble verbs)
meaning: Some common verbs have their own humble forms. They lower your own side's actions to show respect to the listener.
connection: Replace the original verb (行く・来る→参る, 言う→申す, する→いたす, etc.)

senses.label: 参る
senses.meaning: Humble form of 「行く」 and 「来る」, for your own coming and going. In station announcements, 「電車が参ります」 is simply a polite style, not humility.
senses.connection: 参ります／参りました; 〜て参ります
examples: I will come to your office at ten tomorrow.
Someone from our staff will be with you shortly.
The train will be arriving shortly.

senses.label: 申す・申し上げる
senses.meaning: Humble forms of 「言う」. 「申す」 is used for things like giving your name. 「申し上げる」 is directed at someone higher and is more formal; common in thanks and apologies.
senses.connection: 〜と申します; お礼／お詫びを申し上げます
examples: Nice to meet you. My name is Yamada.
I would like to express my heartfelt thanks.

senses.label: いたす
senses.meaning: Humble form of 「する」, for things you do. 「お／ご〜いたします」 is a very common humble pattern.
senses.connection: いたします／いたしました; Sino-Japanese noun + いたします
examples: Well then, I will explain.
Thank you in advance for your help.

senses.label: 伺う
senses.meaning: Humble form of 「聞く」, 「訪ねる」, and 「行く」. Used for asking someone something or visiting them.
senses.connection: 伺います／伺ってもよろしいですか; お話を伺う
examples: I will visit your company tomorrow.
May I ask you a few questions?

senses.label: 拝見する・存じる
senses.meaning: 「拝見する」 is the humble form of 「見る」. 「存じる」 is the humble form of 「知る」 and 「思う」, often as 「存じております」 or 「存じません」.
senses.connection: 拝見します; 存じております／存じません／〜と存じます
examples: I have read your letter.
I am well aware of that matter.

notes: Use them only for yourself or your side. Using them for the other person puts them down: ✕「先生は何と申しましたか」→ ○「何とおっしゃいましたか」; ✕ (asking the listener)「明日は何時に参りますか」→ ○「何時にいらっしゃいますか」.
When mentioning people from your own company to outsiders (even the president), use humble language and drop 「さん」: ✕「社長の田中さんがいらっしゃいます」→ ○「社長の田中が参ります」.

「申す」 is for telling the listener about your side; 「申し上げる」 is for speaking directly to the person who receives the action (a superior or client). Introducing yourself: 「山田と申します」, ✕「山田と申し上げます」; reporting to your boss: 「ご報告申し上げます」.
「参る」 also means "to be beaten, can't take it anymore": 「この暑さには参った」 means "this heat is killing me", and 「参りました」 in a match means "I give up", not "I've come".
「拝見する」 and 「伺う」 are already humble; adding 「させていただく」 is overdoing it. 「拝見させていただきます」 is often heard, but many people see it as excessive honorifics; 「拝見します」 is enough.

etymology: 「参る」 originally meant “to go to a sacred or noble place, to worship”; the 「参」 in 「参拝」 has the same sense. 「申す」 originally meant to state something to a superior. 「いたす」 is written 「致す」 and originally meant “to bring about, to cause to reach”. 「伺う」 originally meant “to look into, to check on (a superior's situation)”.
formation: These were all ordinary verbs meaning "to do something toward a superior" that later became fixed as humble verbs. 「参る」 originally meant "to go to a noble place" (as in 「参拝」), so using it for your own coming and going adds the humble sense of "coming to you". 「申す」 originally meant "to state to a superior"; 「申し上げる」 adds 「上げる」 ("upward") for even more respect. 「いたす（致す）」 originally meant "to cause to arrive, to deliver"; used in place of 「する」, it presents your action as "serving you". 「伺う」 originally meant "to look into or inquire about a superior's situation", which is why it can mean "to visit" and "to ask". The 「拝」 in 「拝見」 means "reverently", so it is "to look reverently". Since their meaning assumes "you are above, I am below", these verbs can only be used for your own side.

similar.title: いらっしゃる・おっしゃる (special respectful verbs)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: they also replace common verbs like 「行く」 and 「言う」, but respectful verbs raise the other person's actions while humble verbs lower your own. For "go": use 「いらっしゃる」 for the other person, 「参る」 or 「伺う」 for yourself.

similar.title: お〜する・ご〜する (humble)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: the humble formula for ordinary verbs. When a verb has a special humble form, use that first: for 「見る」 say 「拝見する」, not 「お見しする」.

similar.title: 〜さしあげる・いただく・くださる (honorific giving and receiving)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「いただく」 (eat, drink, receive) and 「さしあげる」 (give) are also special humble verbs, used specifically for giving and receiving or for eating and drinking, e.g. 「お土産をいただきました」.

similar.title: 〜でございます・〜ております (polite language)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: like 「参る」 and 「いたす」, 「おります」 and 「〜ております」 make statements about your side more formal, and they are often used together: 「担当の者が参っております」. The difference is that polite language (teineigo) only raises the level of politeness and doesn't necessarily involve anyone in particular.

title: 〜でございます・〜ております (polite language)
meaning: More formal versions of 「です」 and 「〜ている」. Used to speak politely to clients or in formal settings.
connection: Noun / na-adjective + でございます; verb te-form + おります

senses.label: でございます
senses.meaning: The formal version of 「です」. It doesn't raise or lower anyone; it just makes the sentence very polite. Common with shop staff, announcements, and formal speeches.
senses.connection: Noun + でございます／でございました／ではございません; 〜でございますか
examples: This is the meeting room.
Your total is 3,000 yen.
We're very sorry, but we are fully booked today.

senses.label: ております
senses.meaning: The formal version of 「〜ています」, used for your own side's actions or states. Extremely common in business emails.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + おります／おりました／おりません (お待ちしております, 存じております)
examples: We look forward to hearing from you.
The person in charge is away from their desk at the moment.

senses.label: おります
senses.meaning: The formal version of 「います」, used to say that you or someone on your side is somewhere. Not used for the other person.
senses.connection: 〜に／は + おります／おりました／おりません
examples: My father is at home now.
Tanaka is not in today.

notes: 「おる」 is humble, so don't use it for the other person: ✕ (asking someone from another company)「社長はおりますか」→ ○「社長はいらっしゃいますか」.
Don't use 「でございます」 to describe the other person themselves: ✕「お客様は田中様でございますか」→ ○「田中様でいらっしゃいますか」. The former sounds as if you were introducing the customer as an item.
「ございます」 on its own means 「あります」; only with 「で」 does it mean 「です」: 「お手洗いはあちらにございます」 (it's over there)／「こちらがお手洗いでございます」 (this is the restroom). Dropping or adding 「で」 changes the meaning.
I-adjectives can't take 「でございます」 directly: ✕「高いでございます」→ ○「高うございます」. That form is old-fashioned; in everyday speech 「高いです」 is fine.
Using 「ございます」 all the time with close coworkers or friends sounds distant or even sarcastic. In everyday conversation, 「です」 and 「います」 are enough.

etymology: 「ござる」 is a contraction of 「御座ある」 (a noble person is seated). It later became a general formal word for 「ある」 and 「いる」, and 「でござる」 turned into 「でございます」. 「おる」 is the old verb 「居る（をり）」; in modern speech it has a humble, formal flavor.
formation: 「でございます」 = copula 「で」 + 「ござる」 + 「ます」. 「ござる」 is a contraction of 「御座ある」, literally "(a noble person's) seat is here", which later became a general formal word for 「ある」. So 「でございます」 replaces the 「ある」 in 「である」 ("to be") with the more formal 「ござる」, parallel to 「である→です」 but more polite. 「ております」 = te-form + 「おる」 + 「ます」, replacing the 「いる」 in 「ている」 with the humble-tinged 「おる」. Since only existence verbs like 「ある」 and 「いる」 are replaced, the pattern doesn't elevate anyone; it just makes speech formal. But 「おる」 carries a humble nuance, so 「おります」 can only be used for your own side.

similar.title: 〜だ・〜です
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「です」 is standard polite speech; 「でございます」 is more formal and used mainly in service industries, announcements and formal settings. 「です」 is enough for everyday conversation with your boss.

similar.title: 〜ございます (polite form of ある)
similar.explanation: Same origin: both come from 「ござる」. 「ございます」 alone corresponds to 「あります」; 「でございます」 corresponds to 「です」. 「駅はあちらにございます」／「こちらが駅でございます」.

similar.title: 〜ている
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「ております」 is the formal version of 「ています」 and is used only for your own side; for the other person, use 「〜ていらっしゃいます」.

title: お〜・ご〜 (beautifying prefixes)
meaning: Adding 「お」 or 「ご」 before a noun makes speech sound refined and polite. With things that belong to the other person, it also shows respect.
connection: お + native Japanese noun／ご + Sino-Japanese noun

senses.label: お + native Japanese noun
senses.meaning: Usually goes with native Japanese words (kun-reading words). It makes speech sound refined, and isn't always about the listener; everyday items often take it too. Some words are fixed and rarely used without it.
senses.connection: お茶, お水, お金, お酒, お皿, お弁当, お風呂, お菓子
examples: Please have some tea.
I don't have enough money.
I take a bath every night.

senses.label: ご + Sino-Japanese noun
senses.meaning: Usually goes with Sino-Japanese words (on-reading words). Words like 「ご飯」 have become completely ordinary. With the other person's things, it shows respect.
senses.connection: ご飯, ご家族, ご両親, ご住所, ご意見, ご連絡
examples: Dinner's ready!
How is your family?

senses.label: The other person's things
senses.meaning: Added to the other person's things or actions to show respect. Normally not used for your own things; when introducing yourself, you don't say 「私のお名前」.
senses.connection: お名前, お仕事, お電話, お時間, ご住所, ご予定
examples: Could you tell me your name?
Do you have time?
Please let me know your schedule.

notes: Don't usually add it to your own things: ✕「私のお名前は王です」→ ○「私の名前は王です」. Add it only when your action concerns the other person, as in 「お電話します」 or 「ご連絡します」.
Loanwords usually don't take it: ✕「おビール」「おコーヒー」「おパソコン」. You may occasionally hear these in service jobs or in some women's casual speech, but learners shouldn't imitate them.
Adding 「お／ご」 can completely change the meaning: 「手洗い」 is "hand washing" but 「お手洗い」 is "restroom"; 「かず」 is "number" but 「おかず」 is "side dish"; 「飯」 is a very rough word, while 「ご飯」 is the normal word.
In principle, native Japanese words take 「お」 and Sino-Japanese words take 「ご」, but some Sino-Japanese words customarily take 「お」: 「お電話」「お時間」「お元気」「お食事」「お料理」; ✕「ご電話」「ご時間」. Memorize these by usage.
Overusing 「お」 sounds affected or childish, e.g. 「お大根」「おにんじん」. Men often drop it in casual settings (「腹」「酒」), but with outsiders and at work it's better to add it.

etymology: Both 「お」 and 「ご」 come from the kanji 「御」. 「お」 is the native reading (「おほみ→おん→お」) and 「ご」 is the Chinese-derived reading, which is why they tend to go with native and Sino-Japanese words respectively. At first they only showed respect; later they also came to simply make speech sound refined.
formation: 「お」 and 「ご」 are two readings of the kanji 「御」: 「お」 comes from the native Japanese reading (おほみ→おん→お), and 「ご」 is the Sino-Japanese (on) reading. So they naturally pair with words of the same type: native words take the native 「お」, Sino-Japanese words take the on-reading 「ご」. 「御」 originally meant "belonging to a noble person", so attaching it to the other person's things shows respect (「お名前」 = your name). With long use the respect wore off, and attached to ordinary things it only makes the wording refined; this is beautifying language (「お茶」, 「お金」). So the same 「お」 is respectful for the other person's things but merely beautifying for everyday items; it depends on whose thing you're talking about.

similar.title: お〜する・ご〜する (humble)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the same 「お／ご」 from 「御」, but here it attaches to a verb's masu-stem and forms a humble pattern with 「する」; the beautifying 「お／ご」 only goes before nouns. 「お茶」 (beautifying)／「お持ちする」 (humble).

similar.title: お〜になる
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「お」 attaches to a verb and, together with 「になる」, forms respectful language for the other person's actions, as in 「お帰りになる」. The beautifying 「お」 attaches to nouns, and 「お帰り」 has become a fixed greeting.

similar.title: 〜でございます・〜ております (polite language)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both just make speech more polite without raising or lowering any particular person. Beautifying language works on a single noun, 「でございます」 on the whole sentence ending.

title: 〜ろ・〜え (imperative form)
meaning: The imperative form of a verb gives a strong, blunt command. It is also used in cheers, signs, and when quoting a command.
connection: Godan verbs: change the final sound to the え-row (行く→行け); ichidan verbs: drop る, add ろ (見る→見ろ); する→しろ／せよ; 来る→来い

senses.label: Strong command
senses.meaning: A direct order. Very strong and rough. Mostly used by men toward younger people, in emergencies, or in fights. Never use it to superiors or strangers.
senses.connection: Godan: 書け, 待て, 帰れ; ichidan: 起きろ, やめろ; する→しろ; 来る→来い
examples: Get up already!
Come over here!
Watch out, run!

senses.label: Cheers and slogans
senses.meaning: Used in cheering at sports, slogans, and traffic signs. It isn't aimed at a particular person, so it isn't rude.
senses.connection: Set phrases like 頑張れ, 負けるな, 止まれ
examples: Go for it! Almost there!
Stop when the light is red.

senses.label: Quoting a command
senses.meaning: When quoting someone's order, use the imperative + 「と」. The sentence itself isn't rude; it just reports what was ordered.
senses.connection: Imperative + と言われた／と言った
examples: My dad told me to go to bed early.
The teacher told me to hand in my homework.

senses.label: Written instructions
senses.meaning: Exam questions and regulations use 「〜せよ」 and 「〜よ」. The tone is neutral and impersonal.
senses.connection: する→せよ; ichidan verbs: drop る, add よ (答えよ, 述べよ)
examples: Answer the following questions.
Explain the underlined part.

notes: The imperative is very blunt. Using it with superiors, elders, guests or strangers comes across as rude or even provocative. To ask someone to do something, use 「〜てください」, or 「〜て」 with people you know well: ✕「ちょっと待て」→ ○「ちょっと待ってください」.
「頑張れ」 is encouragement for peers or juniors; said to superiors or elders it sounds condescending. Use 「頑張ってください」, and with clients 「ご活躍をお祈りしております」 is even better.
Don't confuse godan and ichidan forms: 「見る」→「見ろ」 (✕「見れ」); 「帰る」 is godan →「帰れ」 (✕「帰ろ」). 「帰ろ」 is a casual contraction of the volitional 「帰ろう」 and means "let's go home".
The imperative of 「くれる」 is 「くれ」 (✕「くれろ」). 「〜てくれ」 is still blunt and can't be used with superiors.

etymology: The え-row ending of godan imperatives comes from the imperative of classical yodan verbs. Classical ichidan verbs used 「〜よ」 (見よ); in eastern Japan this became 「〜ろ」 (見ろ) in speech, while 「〜よ」 survives in writing. 「せよ」 is the classical imperative of 「す」.
formation: The imperative is a conjugated form of the verb itself, not something built by adding another word: godan verbs change their ending to the e-row (書く→書け), and ichidan verbs drop 「る」 and add 「ろ」 (見る→見ろ). In old Japanese, the ichidan imperative was 「〜よ」 (見よ), and this 「よ」 is generally thought to be related to an exclamatory particle used to call out to someone. So the imperative is essentially "shouting the action straight at the other person"; in Kanto colloquial speech, 「よ」 became 「ろ」. It throws the bare action at the listener with no request or politeness attached, which makes it the most direct and forceful tone. For the same reason, it sounds concise and powerful in slogans and signs not aimed at anyone in particular. Written forms like 「せよ」 and 「答えよ」 keep the old form, so they sound like formal instructions.

similar.title: 〜なさい
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both are commands. 「なさい」 is a gentle command from parents to children or teachers to students, much softer than the imperative: 「早く寝なさい」 is gentler than 「早く寝ろ」.

similar.title: 〜てください
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both ask someone to do something. 「〜てください」 is a polite request you can use with anyone; the imperative is only for close relationships, speaking down, or emergencies.

similar.title: 〜てくれと言う・〜なと言う (reported commands)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both can relay someone else's command. 「帰れと言われた」 reproduces the harsh command as is; 「帰ってくれと言われた」 relays a request and sounds softer.

title: 〜な (prohibition)
meaning: 「な」 after a verb's dictionary form is a strong prohibition: “Don't …!”

senses.label: Strong prohibition
senses.meaning: Directly forbids someone from doing something. Rough and forceful; mostly used by men toward younger people or in emergencies.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + な (行くな, 触るな, するな, 来るな)
examples: Don't touch it, it's dangerous!
No smoking here.
Don't ever come back!

senses.label: Encouragement and comfort
senses.meaning: In phrases like 「心配するな」, 「負けるな」, 「泣くな」, it encourages or comforts. The tone is warm but firm.
senses.connection: 心配するな, 負けるな, 泣くな, 気にするな, 諦めるな
examples: Don't worry. It'll work out.
Don't give up! Keep going to the end!

senses.label: Signs and quoting
senses.meaning: Used on signs and warnings (not aimed at anyone in particular), or as 「〜なと言われた」 to report someone's prohibition.
senses.connection: Dictionary form + な (signs); dictionary form + なと言う／なと言われた
examples: Keep off the grass.
My doctor told me not to drink alcohol.

notes: 「な」 must follow the dictionary form: ✕「行かないな」→ ○「行くな」. Note that 「行きな」 (masu-stem + な) means the exact opposite: it is a casual 「行きなさい」, "go".
It is harsh and very rude toward superiors, elders, guests or strangers. The polite version is 「〜ないでください」, and 「〜ないで」 with people you know: ✕ (to a guest)「触るな」→ ○「触らないでください」.

A sentence-final 「な」 can also be an exclamation: 「よく食べるな」 means "wow, you sure eat a lot", not "don't eat". The prohibitive 「な」 is short and sharp; the exclamatory 「な」 can also follow adjectives and 「だ」, and is often stretched into 「なあ」.
Don't write 「〜な」 on signs for customers; 「〜ないでください」, 「〜はご遠慮ください」 or 「〜禁止」 is more appropriate.

etymology: Prohibitive 「な」 is a sentence-ending particle from classical Japanese. In old Japanese the form 「な〜そ」 was common (「な行きそ」 = don't go); later it simplified to 「〜な」 at the end of the sentence.
formation: 「〜な」 = dictionary form + the prohibitive sentence-final particle 「な」. Classical Japanese already had "dictionary (conclusive) form + な" for prohibition, along with a gentler 「な〜そ」 (「な行きそ」 = don't go); only the former survives today. The dictionary form stands for the action itself, and 「な」 attached right after it says "no" to the whole action with no cushioning, which is why it sounds short and harsh. It has nothing to do with the negative 「ない」 and doesn't go through the negative form, so the affirmative dictionary form comes before it; this is exactly where learners most often make connection mistakes.

similar.title: 〜ないでください
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both mean "don't ...". 「〜ないでください」 is a polite request you can use with anyone; 「〜な」 is a rude, direct prohibition.

similar.title: 〜てはいけない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express prohibition. 「〜てはいけない」 states a rule ("you must not ...") and is more objective; 「〜な」 is the speaker directly forbidding something, and is stronger.

similar.title: 〜てくれと言う・〜なと言う (reported commands)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜なと言う」 simply puts the prohibitive 「な」 inside a quotation: 「医者に飲むなと言われた」 (the doctor told me not to drink). A more polite way to report it is 「飲まないように言われた」.

meaning: A fairly gentle command, used from above to below, such as parents to children or teachers to students. Also used in exam instructions.

senses.label: Command from an elder
senses.meaning: Commands or instructions from parents or teachers to children or students. Softer than the imperative form, but still speaking down. Women use it a lot too.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + なさい (早く寝なさい, 勉強しなさい)
examples: Go to bed now.
Eat your vegetables too.
Do your homework before you play.

senses.label: Exam instructions
senses.meaning: Common in instructions on tests and in textbooks. The tone is neutral.
senses.connection: 選びなさい, 書きなさい, 答えなさい
examples: Choose the one correct answer.
Answer the following questions.

senses.label: お〜なさい
senses.meaning: Adding 「お」 makes it softer and more refined. Often heard when older people speak to children.
senses.connection: お + verb masu-stem + なさい (お座りなさい, お入りなさい)
examples: Come now, sit down over here.

notes: Although it comes from the respectful verb 「なさる」, today it is a command from above to below, and using it with superiors, elders or guests is very rude: ✕「部長、こちらにお座りなさい」→ ○「どうぞお座りください」.
It follows the masu-stem: ✕「食べるなさい」「食べてなさい」→ ○「食べなさい」.

Watch out for 「〜な」: 「早く寝な」 (masu-stem + な) is a casual 「寝なさい」, meaning "go to bed early", while 「早く寝るな」 (dictionary form + な) means "don't go to bed early". One small difference in connection gives the opposite meaning.
「ごめんなさい」 and 「おやすみなさい」 are set phrases with no commanding sense. But 「ごめんなさい」 sounds childish when apologizing to a superior or client; say 「申し訳ありません」 instead.

etymology: 「なさい」 is the imperative of the respectful verb 「なさる」 (respectful 「する」). It was originally respectful, but the respect faded and it became a gentle command from above to below.
formation: 「なさい」 is the imperative of the respectful verb 「なさる」 (respectful form of 「する」), attached to the masu-stem: 「食べ」 + 「なさい」, literally "please do the act of 'eating'". Here the masu-stem is the action as a noun and 「なさる」 means "to do", the same logic by which 「お〜になる」 and 「お〜する」 borrow the masu-stem. Giving an order with a respectful verb was originally a way to "command while saving the other person's face", so it is softer than the imperative. With heavy use the respect wore off, leaving only a tone of "from above to below, gentle but not negotiable". 「ごめんなさい」 (「ご免」 + なさい = please forgive me) and 「おやすみなさい」 (please rest) are built the same way, but have become fixed greetings.

similar.title: 〜ろ・〜え (imperative form)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both are commands. The imperative is rude and forceful; 「なさい」 is also a command, but gentle and well-mannered.

similar.title: 〜てください
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both ask someone to do something. 「〜てください」 is a polite request you can use with anyone; 「なさい」 is only used from above to below.

similar.title: お〜ください
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both can be softened with 「お」. 「お座りください」 is a respectful request used for guests and superiors; 「お座りなさい」 is what an elder says to a younger person.

similar.title: いらっしゃる・おっしゃる (special respectful verbs)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「なさい」 is simply the imperative of the special respectful verb 「なさる」. 「何をなさいますか」 (what will you do?) is respectful, while 「勉強しなさい」 (go study) is already a command from above.

title: 〜(よ)う (volitional form)
meaning: The volitional form expresses the speaker's will (“I'll …”) or a suggestion (“Let's …”). It is the plain form of 「ましょう」.
connection: Godan verbs: change the final sound to the お-row + う (行く→行こう); ichidan verbs: drop る, add よう; する→しよう; 来る→来よう

senses.label: Suggestions and invitations
senses.meaning: Invites the other person to do something together: “Let's ….” The plain form of 「〜ましょう」, used with friends and family.
senses.connection: Verb volitional form (行こう, 食べよう, しよう)
examples: Let's go home together.
I'm tired. Let's take a short break.
Let's go see a movie tomorrow.

senses.label: Will and resolve
senses.meaning: The speaker states a decision or intention, often to themselves: “I'll ….” Often used with 「よし」 or 「今日から」.
senses.connection: Verb volitional form (talking to yourself)
examples: Right, starting today I'm going to exercise every day.
It's late, so I'd better go to bed.

senses.label: 〜(よ)うか
senses.meaning: Adding 「か」 offers to do something for the other person, or shows you're undecided: “Shall I …?”, “What should I …?”
senses.connection: Verb volitional form + か (手伝おうか, どうしようか)
examples: Want me to carry your bag?
Hmm, what should I have for lunch?

notes: The volitional form is plain style, so don't use it with superiors or clients: ✕「部長、一緒に行こう」→ ○「ご一緒しませんか」. Even 「〜ましょう」 feels like deciding for the other person; 「〜ませんか」 is more appropriate when inviting a superior.
The volitional expresses the speaker's own will and can't directly express a third person's will: ✕「田中さんは留学しよう」→ ○「田中さんは留学しようと思っている」「留学するつもりだ」.
Don't confuse godan and ichidan: 「帰る」 (godan) →「帰ろう」, 「見る」 (ichidan) →「見よう」; ✕「帰りよう」「見ろう」. 「買う」→「買おう」, ✕「買よう」.
Offering help with 「〜(よ)うか」 is casual: saying 「持とうか」 to a superior or client is impolite; say 「お持ちしましょうか」.

etymology: The volitional form comes from the classical auxiliary 「む」, which expressed conjecture and will. 「む」 changed to 「う」 and merged with the verb: 「行かむ→行かう→行こう」. Ichidan verbs add 「よう」.
formation: Volitional form = verb + 「う」, which evolved from the classical auxiliary 「む」. 「む」 originally marked things not yet realized and covered conjecture, intention and invitation ("probably will ...", "I will ...", "let's ..."). Later 「む」 became 「う」 and merged with the preceding sound: 「行かむ→行かう→行こう」; this is where the godan "o-row + う" comes from, while ichidan verbs use 「よう」 (見よう). Because the core is "it hasn't happened yet, and I want to make it happen", used for yourself it is a resolution (「やろう」), and pulling the listener in makes it an invitation (「行こう」). In modern speech, conjecture has been handed over to 「だろう」, so the volitional mainly keeps intention and invitation.

similar.title: 〜ましょう
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜ましょう」 is polite style and 「〜(よ)う」 is plain style; for invitations and intentions they mean basically the same thing.

similar.title: 〜ましょうか (offers and suggestions)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「持とうか」 and 「お持ちしましょうか」 both offer help; the former is for friends and family, the latter for superiors and guests.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うと思う
similar.explanation: Same origin: formed by adding 「と思う」 to the volitional form. 「〜(よ)う」 is a decision or suggestion made on the spot; 「〜(よ)うと思う」 tells others about your plans.

similar.title: 〜つもりだ
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express intention. 「つもり」 is a plan decided in advance and can be used for third persons; the volitional is mostly a decision or suggestion made at the moment of speaking.

title: 〜ように言う (indirect command)
meaning: Reports an instruction, request, or piece of advice: “tell (someone) to …”, “ask (someone) to ….”
connection: Verb dictionary form／nai-form + ように + 言う／頼む／伝える, etc.

senses.label: Telling someone to do something
senses.meaning: Reports the content of an order or instruction. Softer than quoting the imperative directly. The passive 「〜ように言われた」 (“I was told to …”) is very common.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form／nai-form + ように言う／言われる
examples: My teacher told me to practice kanji every day.
Mom told my little brother not to play video games.
The doctor told me to go to bed early.

senses.label: Requests
senses.meaning: Reports what you asked someone to do. Followed by 「頼む」 or 「お願いする」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form／nai-form + ように頼む／お願いする
examples: I asked a friend to come pick me up at the station.
I asked the manager to check the materials.

senses.label: Passing on messages and warnings
senses.meaning: Followed by 「伝える」, 「注意する」, 「指示する」, etc. to pass on a message or warning. 「〜ように伝えてください」 is very common.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form／nai-form + ように伝える／注意する／指示する
examples: Please tell Mr. Tanaka to call me later.
I warned the children not to play in the street.

notes: 「ように言う」 reports "telling someone to do something"; to simply report what someone said, use 「と言う」: 「田中さんは明日来るように言った」 means "Tanaka told (someone) to come tomorrow", while 「田中さんは明日来ると言った」 means "Tanaka said he would come tomorrow".
「ように」 only follows the dictionary form or nai-form: ✕「早く寝てように言った」→ ○「早く寝るように言った」; the negative is 「〜ないように」, ✕「遅れないでように」.

In the passive 「〜ように言われた」, the person making the request is marked with 「に」: 「先生に早く来るように言われた」 (the teacher told me to come early). If you write 「先生が早く来るように言われた」, it means "the teacher was told to come early".
When reporting to a superior, don't say you "told" your boss to do something: ✕「部長に資料を確認するように言いました」→ ○「部長に資料のご確認をお願いしました」.

etymology: 「ように」 is the formal noun 「よう」 (manner, way; written 「様」) plus the particle 「に」. It originally meant “(do it) in the manner of ….” Followed by a verb of speaking, it came to report instructions.
formation: 「ように」 = formal noun 「よう（様）」 + case particle 「に」. 「様」 means "appearance, manner", so 「〜ように」 is "in the manner of ...". Followed by 「言う」, 「頼む」 or 「伝える」, it literally means "say in the manner of 'do ...'": it only conveys the state you want the other person to reach, without reproducing the tone of the order, so it is indirect speech and softer than 「〜ろと言う」. And because 「ように」 points to a state that hasn't happened yet but is hoped for, only the dictionary form or nai-form can come before it, never the past. This is the same "working toward a state" meaning found in 「ように」 (purpose) and 「ようにする」.

similar.title: 〜てくれと言う・〜なと言う (reported commands)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both relay someone's request. 「〜てくれと言われた」 keeps the requesting tone of the original words; 「〜ように言われた」 only relays the content, which is more objective and softer and suits formal settings.

similar.title: 〜と言う (quotation)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「と言う」 quotes the original words directly (it can even take the imperative: 「寝ろと言った」); 「ように言う」 reports the instruction indirectly and sounds softer.

similar.title: 〜ように (purpose)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the same 「ように」, meaning "so as to reach a certain state", followed by an ordinary action: 「忘れないようにメモする」; this pattern, by contrast, is followed by speech verbs like 「言う」 or 「頼む」.

similar.title: 〜ようにする
similar.explanation: Same origin: the same 「ように」. 「ようにする」 is making an effort yourself; 「ように言う」 is telling someone else to do it.

title: 〜ような・〜ように・〜みたいな (comparison, examples)
meaning: Compares something to something else (“like …”), or gives an example (“such as …”). 「みたいな」 is the casual form.
connection: Noun + の／verb plain form + ような (+ noun)・ように (+ predicate); noun + みたいな・みたいに

senses.label: Comparison
senses.meaning: Compares A to B, which has a similar quality: “like ….” Often paired with 「まるで」. 「ような」 modifies nouns; 「ように」 modifies verbs and adjectives.
senses.connection: Noun + の + ような + noun; noun + の + ように + predicate (まるで〜のような／ように)
examples: It was a day just like a dream.
He laughed like a child.
Skin as white as snow.

senses.label: Giving examples
senses.meaning: Gives a concrete example of a type of thing: “such as …, like ….” A stands for the type that B belongs to.
senses.connection: Noun + の + ような + noun (東京のような大都市)
examples: I want to live in a big city like Tokyo.
I like Japanese food such as sushi and tempura.

senses.label: As, the same as usual
senses.meaning: 「〜のように」 and verb + 「ように」 can also mean “as …, in the way that ….” E.g. 「いつものように」 = “as usual”.
senses.connection: Noun + の + ように; いつものように, このように
examples: I got up at seven as usual.
Please write it like this.

senses.label: Casual みたいな
senses.meaning: 「みたいな」 and 「みたいに」 are the casual forms of 「ような」 and 「ように」. They attach directly to nouns, without 「の」.
senses.connection: Noun + みたいな + noun; noun + みたいに + predicate
examples: I want to be someone like my older sister.
It's hot like summer today, isn't it?

notes: After a noun, 「ような／ように」 needs 「の」, but 「みたいな／みたいに」 does not: ✕「夢ような」「夢のみたいな」→ ○「夢のような」「夢みたいな」.
Use 「ような」 to modify nouns and 「ように」 to modify verbs and adjectives: ✕「子供のような笑った」→ ○「子供のように笑った」.
「みたい」 is colloquial; in reports, business documents and formal settings, use 「ような」: ✕ (in a report)「前年みたいな結果になった」→ ○「前年のような結果になった」.
To praise a man as manly, say 「男らしい」. 「男のような」 means "like a man (but not actually one)"; used about a woman, it may be taken as negative, so be careful.
Sentence-final 「〜ようだ」 and 「〜みたいだ」 usually express conjecture: 「雪のようだ」 can mean either "like snow" or "it seems to be snow". To make a comparison clear, add 「まるで」.

etymology: 「よう」 is written 「様」 and originally meant “appearance, state”. 「ような」 is the attributive form of 「様だ」 and 「ように」 is its adverbial form. 「みたい」 is said to be a contraction of 「〜を見たような」 (one theory) and became common in speech from the Edo period on.
formation: 「ような」 and 「ように」 come from the noun 「様（よう）」 plus the assertive auxiliary: the attributive form of 「様だ」 is 「様な」 and its continuative form is 「様に」. 「様」 means "appearance, state", so 「AのようなB」 is literally "B with A's appearance", which can mean "looking like A" (comparison) or "of A's kind" (example). Because 「様」 is originally a noun, a preceding noun needs 「の」 to modify it, which is why 「夢のような」 must have 「の」. 「みたい」 is generally thought to be a contraction of 「〜を見たような」; it has become an adjective-like word that attaches directly to nouns, so 「夢みたいな」 takes no 「の」.

similar.title: 〜ようだ・〜みたいだ
similar.explanation: Same origin: the same 「様」. At the end of a sentence, 「ようだ」 and 「みたいだ」 usually express conjecture ("it seems ..."); within a sentence, 「ような」 and 「ように」 modify nouns or predicates and mainly express comparison or examples.

similar.title: 〜かのようだ
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express comparison. 「〜かのようだ」 stresses "as if ..., though it isn't really so", usually follows a verb clause and is rather written: 「何もなかったかのように笑った」; 「のような」 usually follows nouns and is more everyday.

similar.title: 〜らしい (typical, befitting)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both can be translated as "like ...". 「男らしい」 means "manly" (he is a man); 「男のような」 compares someone to a man (they aren't one).

meaning: Special forms when 「そう」 (looks like) attaches to 「ない」 and 「いい」: “doesn't seem to have …”, “looks good”.
connection: ない → なさそう; いい／よい → よさそう; 〜くない → 〜くなさそう

senses.label: よさそう
senses.meaning: When 「いい」 takes 「そう」 (looks like), it becomes 「よさそう」: “looks good, seems nice”. ✕「いさそう」.
senses.connection: よさそうだ／よさそうな + noun; 〜てもよさそうだ
examples: This place looks good.
The weather looks nice, so let's go for a walk.
This looks easy to use. It seems good.

senses.label: なさそう
senses.meaning: When 「ない」 (there isn't) takes 「そう」, it becomes 「なさそう」: “doesn't seem to have ….”
senses.connection: Noun + が + なさそうだ (お金がなさそう, 時間がなさそう)
examples: He doesn't seem to have much money.
Looks like we don't have time today.

senses.label: Negative appearance
senses.meaning: The negative forms of adjectives and nouns also become 「なさそう」 with 「そう」: 「おいしくない→おいしくなさそう」, 「学生じゃない→学生じゃなさそう」.
senses.connection: i-adjective く + なさそう; noun / na-adjective + じゃ／では + なさそう
examples: This cake doesn't look very sweet.
That person doesn't seem to be Japanese.

notes: 「いい」 and 「ない」 need 「さ」 before the 「そう」 of appearance: ✕「いいそうだ」→ ○「よさそうだ」. 「いいそうだ」 and 「ないそうだ」 are hearsay, meaning "I hear it's good" and "I hear there isn't any".
For a negative adjective, the appearance form is 「〜くなさそう」: ○「おいしくなさそう」 (doesn't look tasty); ✕「おいしくないそう」 is hearsay: "I hear it isn't tasty".
For a negative verb, the standard form is 「〜なそう」: 「雨は降らなそうだ」. 「降らなさそう」 is also very common in speech, but exams treat 「なそう」 as correct.
「よさそう」 implies "judging from appearances, not yet confirmed". Saying 「よさそうですね」 about your superior's proposal can sound like you're grading it; 「いいですね」 or 「素晴らしいと思います」 is more appropriate.

etymology: 「そう」 (looks like) attaches to the adjective stem. The stems of 「いい」 and 「ない」 are just one syllable, so 「さ」 was inserted for stability, giving 「よさそう」 and 「なさそう」. The 「よ」 comes from 「よい」, the older form of 「いい」.
formation: The 「そう」 of appearance attaches to an adjective's stem (高い→高そう). The old form of 「いい」 is 「よい」, whose stem is 「よ」; the stem of 「ない」 is 「な」. Both stems are just one syllable, and attaching them directly as 「よそう」 or 「なそう」 is generally thought to be too short and unstable, so 「さ」 is inserted to fill out the syllable: 「よさ＋そう」, 「なさ＋そう」. So 「さ」 is just the special form used when the 「そう」 of appearance attaches to these two words. The hearsay 「そうだ」 attaches to the full plain form (「いいそうだ」) and needs no 「さ」; this is the key formal difference between the two kinds of 「そうだ」.

similar.title: 〜そうだ (appearance)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「よさそう」 and 「なさそう」 are special forms of the 「そうだ」 of appearance. Ordinary adjectives drop 「い」 and add 「そう」 directly (高そう); 「いい」 and 「ない」 are exceptions that need 「さ」.

similar.title: 〜そうもない・〜そうにない
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are built with the 「そう」 of appearance. 「なさそう」 means "doesn't seem to be/have"; 「〜そうもない」 follows verbs and means "doesn't look like it will happen": 「雨はやみそうもない」.

similar.title: 〜ようだ・〜みたいだ
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both can express conjecture. 「よさそう」 is a direct impression from appearance; 「いいようだ」 is a judgment based on various circumstances and is more objective.

similar.title: 〜らしい
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both can express conjecture. 「いいらしい」 is usually based on information you heard; 「よさそう」 is a direct impression from what you saw yourself.

meaning: Gives the source of news or information: “according to ….” The second half usually ends with 「そうだ」, 「らしい」, or 「ということだ」.
connection: Noun + によると／によれば

senses.label: Source of information
senses.meaning: Introduces where the information comes from, like the news, a forecast, or what someone said. The second half usually matches with hearsay endings like 「〜そうだ」, 「〜らしい」, 「〜ということだ」.
senses.connection: Noun + によると, 〜そうだ／らしい (天気予報によると, ニュースによると)
examples: According to the weather forecast, it's going to rain tomorrow.
According to the news, there was an accident in front of the station.
According to a friend, that shop is closing next month.

senses.label: Surveys and data
senses.meaning: Introduces evidence such as surveys or statistics. 「によれば」 means the same as 「によると」 but sounds a bit more formal. Common in news and reports.
senses.connection: Survey / statistics / report (調査／統計／報告) + によれば, 〜という
examples: According to a survey, young people are spending less time reading.
According to the police, no one was injured.

notes: End the sentence with a hearsay expression (「〜そうだ」「〜らしい」「〜ということだ」「〜とのことだ」); otherwise it sounds as if you're asserting it yourself: ✕「天気予報によると、明日は雨です」→ ○「明日は雨だそうです」.
The second part can't be the speaker's intention, invitation or request: ✕「ニュースによると、傘を持っていこう」→ ○「ニュースによると雨らしいから、傘を持っていこう」.

「によると」 and 「によって」 mean different things, and mixing them up changes the meaning: 「先生によると、試験は来週だ」 means "according to the teacher"; 「先生によって説明が違う」 means "the explanation differs from teacher to teacher".

etymology: 「よる」 is written 「拠る・依る」 and means “to rely on, to be based on”. 「によると」 is 「による」 + the conditional 「と」, and 「によれば」 uses the ば-conditional. Literally: “if we go by ….”
formation: 「によると」 = case particle 「に」 + the verb 「よる」 (拠る・依る: to be based on) + the conditional particle 「と」; 「によれば」 just swaps 「と」 for the conditional 「〜ば」. Literally "if based on ...", it first declares "what I'm saying has a source", so the second part naturally ends with a hearsay expression: the speaker only relays the information without vouching for it. The same 「による」 in te-form becomes 「によって」 (means, cause), and in attributive form 「〜による」 + noun (「地震による被害」); they are one family. Only the conditional form specializes in information sources, because "if based on ..." is exactly the way to introduce a source.

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: Same origin: also from 「よる」 (to be based on). 「によって」 marks means, cause, the agent of a passive, or "varies depending on"; 「によると」 is specifically for the source of information.

similar.title: 〜そうだ (hearsay)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both are used for hearsay and often appear together: 「によると」 gives the source, and 「そうだ」 at the end of the sentence means "I hear".

similar.title: 〜と聞いた
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both state where information came from. 「〜と聞いた」 stresses that you heard it yourself; 「によると」 can take any source, such as news, surveys or documents, and is more objective.

similar.title: 〜ということだ (hearsay, conclusion)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express hearsay and often go together with 「によると」: 「警察によると、けが人はいないということだ」. 「ということだ」 goes at the end of the sentence, 「によると」 at the beginning.

title: 〜って (quotation, topic)
meaning: In casual speech, 「って」 replaces 「と」 when quoting, or replaces 「は」 or 「というのは」 to bring up a topic.

senses.label: Quoting (= と)
senses.meaning: Replaces quoting 「と」 before 「言う」, 「聞く」, 「思う」, etc. Casual; common among friends.
senses.connection: Plain form + って言う／って聞いた／って思う
examples: Tanaka said he's coming tomorrow.
I heard that restaurant is good.
I thought, “That's it, I can't do this.”

senses.label: Sentence-final reporting
senses.meaning: At the end of a sentence, 「言っていた」 is dropped, leaving “(someone) said ….” Used to pass on a message.
senses.connection: Plain form + って。／ってよ。
examples: Mom says she'll be late today.
The teacher says there's no school tomorrow.

senses.label: Topic (= は)
senses.meaning: Replaces 「は」 or 「というのは」 to bring up a topic, with a nuance of “speaking of …, this thing called ….” Often used for opinions or questions.
senses.connection: Noun／plain form + って + comment or question
examples: Summers in Japan are really hot, aren't they?
What kind of person is Suzuki?
What's this?

senses.label: Called (= という)
senses.meaning: 「っていう」 replaces 「という」 to give a name: “called ….”
senses.connection: Noun + っていう + noun
examples: I have a dog called Pochi.
Someone called Yamada phoned you.

notes: 「って」 is very casual spoken language; using it with superiors, clients or in formal documents is impolite: ✕ (to your boss)「田中さん、今日休むって」→ ○「田中さんから、今日は休むと連絡がありました」.
Sentence-final 「〜って」 relays what someone else said, not your own judgment: 「明日は休みだって」 means "(someone) says tomorrow is a day off". For something you know for sure, say 「明日は休みだよ」.
When relaying at the end of a sentence, nouns and na-adjectives need 「だ」: ○「休みだって」 (I hear it's a day off); ✕「休みって」 instead raises a topic: "speaking of days off ...".
Don't confuse it with the verb te-form: 「行くって」 means "(someone) says they'll go", while 「行って」 is the te-form "go (and then)"; the 「って」 in 「待って」 and 「言って」 is the te-form too.

etymology: 「って」 developed from the quoting particle 「と」, and is generally linked to contractions of 「とて」 and 「と言って」. It spread in speech from the Edo period on, and later also came to replace 「は」 and 「というのは」 to mark topics.
formation: 「って」 is a colloquial variant of the quotative particle 「と」, generally thought to come from contractions of forms like 「と言って」 and 「とて」, with a doubled consonant (small っ). Its core function is "quoting": it frames a piece of content. Followed by 「言う」 or 「聞く」, it is a quotation (＝と), and dropping the following 「言っていた」 turns it into sentence-final relaying. Framing a word and holding it up amounts to saying "the so-called ...", so it can also present a topic (＝というのは／は) with the nuance of "speaking of ...". Followed by 「いう」, it becomes 「っていう」 (＝という, "called"). Since all its uses "quote a piece of content", nouns need 「だ」 when relaying at the end of a sentence, so that the quoted part becomes a complete sentence.

similar.title: 〜と言う (quotation)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「って言う」 is the colloquial version of 「と言う」. 「と言う」 works in formal settings; 「って」 is only for casual speech among people you know.

similar.title: 〜というのは
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: when raising a topic or asking what something means, 「〜って何？」 equals 「〜というのは何ですか」. The latter is more formal and suits superiors or writing.

similar.title: 〜という (called)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「っていう」 is the colloquial form of 「という」 with the same meaning: 「ポチっていう犬」 = 「ポチという犬」.

similar.title: 〜んだって
similar.explanation: Same origin: formed from 「〜んだ」 + sentence-final 「って」, it specifically means "I hear ...", with the nuance of passing new information on to the listener.

meaning: Explains the meaning of a word, sentence, sign, or what someone really means: “it means ….”
connection: Plain form／noun + という意味だ (casual: って意味)

senses.label: Explaining a word
senses.meaning: Explains what a word, kanji, or sign means. The common pattern is 「AはBという意味だ」.
senses.connection: A は B という意味です
examples: 「立入禁止」 means you must not enter.
This symbol means no smoking.

senses.label: Asking what something means
senses.meaning: Use 「どういう意味ですか」 to ask what a word means or what someone meant.
senses.connection: 〜はどういう意味ですか; 〜って、どういう意味？
examples: What does this word mean?
What's that supposed to mean?

senses.label: Implied meaning
senses.meaning: Checks or explains the intention behind what someone said: “Do you mean …?”
senses.connection: Plain form + という意味ですか／という意味ではない
examples: Does that mean you're not going?
I don't mean I dislike it.
You mean I don't have to come anymore?

notes: Saying 「それ、どういう意味？」 or 「どういう意味ですか」 directly about someone's words often sounds like a challenge or complaint; to check gently, say 「〜ということでしょうか」.
Don't repeat 「意味」 at both ends: ✕「この言葉の意味は、〜という意味です」→ ○「この言葉は〜という意味です」 or 「この言葉の意味は〜ということです」.
Use the plain form before 「という」: ✕「入ってはいけませんという意味です」→ ○「入ってはいけないという意味です」.
「意味がある／ない」 means "to have/lack meaning or value", not "to have the meaning of ...": 「この練習は意味がない」 means "this practice is pointless".

etymology: It's quoting 「という」 plus the noun 「意味」 (meaning), literally “the meaning called ….” 「意味」 is a Sino-Japanese word that originally meant “sense, significance”.
formation: 「という意味だ」 = quotative particle 「と」 + 「いう（言う）」 + the noun 「意味」 + 「だ」. 「と」 marks the content of speech and 「いう」 means "say"; 「〜という」 literally means "said to be ...", and came to be used to give the specific content of the following noun (「ポチという犬」). Attached to 「意味」, it means "the meaning called ...", presenting the preceding content as the concrete explanation of 「意味」. So what comes before is a complete "quoted" sentence or word, usually in plain form. Replacing the content with the question word 「どう」 gives the question 「どういう意味」; in speech, 「という」 becomes 「っていう」 or 「って」, giving 「って意味」.

similar.title: 〜という (called)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the same 「という」. 「ポチという犬」 explains a name; 「という意味」 explains a meaning.

similar.title: 〜というのは
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both are used to explain word meanings, often together: 「『立入禁止』というのは、入ってはいけないという意味だ」. 「というのは」 raises the word to be explained; 「という意味だ」 gives the explanation.

similar.title: 〜ということだ (hearsay, conclusion)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: for a conclusion ("in other words ..."), both 「つまり、行かないということですか」 and 「行かないという意味ですか」 can confirm what the other person means; the former is softer and more natural.
